title: CoStar Group Announces Launch of CoStar Platform in France

body_text: CoStar Group Announces Launch of CoStar Platform in France July 2, 2026 PDF Version Empowering investors, brokers, owners, and occupiers with the data and analytics needed to succeed in France’s estimated €300 billion commercial real estate market PARIS--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 2, 2026-- CoStar Group (NASDAQ: CSGP), an S&P 500 company and the global leader in real estate marketplaces, information, analytics and 3D digital twin technology today announces the official launch of the CoStar platform in France – bringing its commercial real estate intelligence platform to one of Europe’s largest markets. The launch builds on CoStar Group’s acquisitions of BureauxLocaux and Business Immo and significant investment in local proprietary research to create one of the most comprehensive commercial property databases ever built for the French market. For the first time, investors, brokers, owners, corporate occupiers, and lenders in France can use a single platform to access curated property records, live availabilities, verified sale/lease comparables, exclusive industry news and real-time market analytics built from the ground up for the French market. The launch was made possible by CoStar Group’s investment of more than $5 billion in proprietary data and technology over four decades to build a proprietary global database that is unmatched in the industry. Globally, the CoStar platform draws on: 9 million properties tracked 8 million commercial tenants and 2 million owners connected to properties 7 million lease activities and 5 million sales comparables 15,000 analytical reports covering markets and submarkets Industry news articles linked directly to properties and people. From launch in France, CoStar will deliver one of the most comprehensive commercial real estate datasets in France spanning office, logistics, and hospitality sectors across the country’s major metropolitan areas – including Greater Paris, Lyon, and Marseille. CoStar clients immediately benefit from more than 290,000 properties tracked, 385,000 commercial tenants, 90,000 availabilities, 75,000 lease activities and sales comparables, over 134 market and submarket analytical reports, and market-leading real estate news. “France is one of the most important real estate markets in the world, and we are delighted to bring to France the same platform that has transformed how commercial real estate is transacted in the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada. French brokers, investors, owners and occupiers will now be able to source opportunities faster, underwrite more robustly and make decisions with greater confidence,” said Andy Florance, Founder and CEO of CoStar Group. “ Commercial real estate operates across borders, and CoStar’s subscriber base of over 320,000 CRE professionals around the world will now find it easier to evaluate opportunities in France, while French CoStar subscribers will be able to access opportunities abroad.” Sandra Roumi, General Manager France of CoStar Group : " French real estate is entering a new era. Our ambition is clear: to support the real estate ecosystem with the highest standards in data quality, transparency, and technology. CoStar Group is investing heavily to build, alongside the French market, a new generation of tools and services designed to support performance, confidence, and growth. " About CoStar Group CoStar Group (NASDAQ: CSGP), an S&P 500 company, is the global leader in commercial real estate information, analytics, online marketplaces, and 3D digital twin technology. Founded in 1986 and headquartered in Arlington, Virginia, CoStar Group has delivered 60 consecutive quarters of double-digit revenue growth, generating $3.2 billion in revenue in 2025. The company has invested more than $5 billion in building its proprietary database, employs over 1,500 researchers worldwide, and operates in more than 15 countries. CoStar Group is dedicated to digitizing the world’s real estate, empowering all people to discover properties, insights, and connections that improve their businesses and lives. CoStar Group’s major brands include CoStar, a leading global provider of commercial real estate data, analytics, and news; LoopNet, the most trafficked commercial real estate marketplace; Apartments.com, the leading platform for apartment rentals; Homes.com, the fastest-growing residential real estate marketplace; and Domain, one of Australia’s leading property marketplaces. CoStar Group’s industry-leading brands also include Matterport, a leading spatial data company whose platform turns buildings into data to make every space more valuable and accessible; STR, a global leader in hospitality data and benchmarking; Ten-X, an online platform for commercial real estate auctions and negotiated bids; and OnTheMarket, a leading residential property portal in the United Kingdom. CoStar Group’s websites attracted 131 million average monthly unique visitors in the first quarter of 2026, serving clients around the world. Headquartered in Arlington, Virginia, CoStar Group is committed to transforming the real estate industry through innovative technology and comprehensive market intelligence. From time to time, we plan to utilize our corporate website as a channel of distribution for material company information. For more information, visit CoStarGroup.com . title: What Is a Reverse-Engineered API Integration? A Plain-Language Guide
summary: Reverse-engineered API integration means accessing a platform's private HTTP endpoints directly, not through a browser. Here's what it actually involves, whether it's legally sound, and how reliable it is for production use.
body_text: The phrase "reverse engineering" carries baggage. It conjures images of hackers, cracked software, and Terms of Service violations. For teams that hear it in the context of API integration, the instinct is to flag it as a legal or technical risk and move on to safer options. That instinct is worth examining, because in practice, reverse-engineered API integration is how production engineering teams at healthcare AI companies, logistics platforms, and FinTech startups access the long tail of platforms that built a web application but never built a public API. The technique is specific, well-understood, and used at scale. What it means, in context, is considerably more prosaic than the name suggests. What Is a Reverse-Engineered API Integration? A reverse-engineered API integration is a programmatic connection to a web platform built by analyzing the platform's own network traffic: identifying the private HTTP endpoints its frontend calls, documenting their structure and authentication requirements, and then calling those endpoints directly rather than through a browser. The result behaves exactly like a REST API: it accepts HTTP requests, returns structured JSON, and is callable from any standard HTTP client or application code. Every modern web application built as a Single-Page Application communicates with its own backend through HTTP requests. The React or Angular interface your team logs into every day is just a client calling real endpoints with real request and response schemas. Those endpoints exist whether the platform publishes a developer API or not. Reverse-engineering finds them and formalizes the contract. What it is not: it has nothing to do with decompiling binaries, cracking encryption, or accessing any data the account holder does not have legitimate permission to access. You are reproducing calls that your own browser already makes, on behalf of an authenticated user account you own. How It Actually Works The process follows a consistent sequence, whether done manually by an engineer or automated by a platform like Integuru: Authenticate with the target platform. The integration operates inside a real, authenticated session using credentials you own. No credentials are guessed or bypassed. Observe the network traffic. With browser DevTools open and the Fetch/XHR filter active, navigate through the workflows you need to automate. Each action generates visible HTTP requests, complete with URL, method, headers, request body, and response schema. Identify the relevant endpoints. Isolate the API calls from static asset loading. Note the URL patterns, HTTP methods, authentication headers, and JSON payloads for each action you need. Map the authentication flow. Capture how the platform manages sessions: cookie-based sessions, bearer tokens, OAuth handshakes, and any 2FA verification steps. Authentication handling is the most common production failure point and needs to be treated explicitly. Replay and verify. Test the captured endpoints outside the browser using curl or a REST client. A consistent 200 response confirms the endpoint is callable without any browser involvement. Document and wrap. Record request and response schemas, error codes, and rate limits. Wrap the endpoints in a stable interface with proper error handling. At Integuru, we automate steps 2 through 6. You authenticate; our agent analyzes the platform's network traffic, maps the endpoint structure, handles the authentication flow, and delivers production-ready documented endpoints within 10 to 20 minutes. Is It Legally and Ethically Sound? This is the question most enterprise buyers ask first, and it deserves a direct answer rather than a deflection. Much of the legal anxiety around "reverse engineering" comes from a different context entirely: binary decompilation, where courts and the DMCA have drawn hard lines around extracting proprietary logic from compiled software. HTTP traffic observation is categorically different. You are not extracting software; you are reading network packets your own browser generates on your own network connection, authenticated with credentials you own. The server sent you this data. You are replaying the same request. The user-permissioned model is categorically different from unauthorized access. You are logging in with credentials you own, navigating a platform your team has legitimate access to, and reproducing HTTP calls that your own authenticated browser session already makes. You are not bypassing authentication, accessing other users' data, or extracting anything the server has not already chosen to send to your account. Courts have engaged with related questions. In hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn (9th Circuit, 2022), the court found that scraping publicly accessible data does not violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, noting that the CFAA was designed to target unauthorized access, not access to data a server makes available. User-permissioned access to private account data sits on considerably firmer ground than public scraping, because the authorization is explicit. That said, legal analysis always depends on jurisdiction, specific platform Terms of Service, the nature of the data involved, and how the integration is used commercially. At Integuru, we operate the user-permissioned model by design. We do not provide legal advice and neither does this post. Consult legal counsel for your specific use case before deploying any integration that touches regulated data or operates under commercial terms that warrant review. The ethical position is straightforward: you are accessing your own data, on your own account, for your own business purposes, via the same mechanism the platform's interface uses. Is It Reliable for Production Use? The common objection is brittleness: "won't it break every time the platform updates?" The concern is understandable, but it conflates two different integration approaches that operate at different layers of the stack. Reverse-engineered API integrations target the data layer, not the UI layer. A platform redesign changes CSS, HTML structure, and component names. It does not, in most cases, change the backend JSON endpoints the frontend was calling. Browser-based automation (Selenium, Puppeteer, Playwright) is coupled to the visual layer. A button rename, a CSS class change, a DOM restructure, and the integration breaks. The platform did not change its API; it changed its interface. To browser automation, those look the same. Direct HTTP integration is coupled to the backend contract: the endpoint URL, the request schema, and the response format. Backend contracts are significantly more stable than frontend markup. Platforms iterate on their UI far more frequently than on the underlying API their own frontend depends on. At Integuru, across production deployments, the integrations we maintain hit 99.9%+ reliability with average response times under 3 seconds . There is no browser load cycle adding latency. The integration calls the endpoint directly and returns structured data. When backend endpoints do change, that is what our 24/7 on-call maintenance team handles. Platform updates their auth flow or restructures an endpoint: our team detects the breakage, repairs the integration, and restores service. Your engineering backlog does not absorb it. Key metrics across Integuru production integrations: 99.9%+ reliability rate Under 3 seconds average response time 24/7 on-call maintenance for endpoint and auth changes 10-20 minutes to generate production-ready endpoints for a new platform How Reverse-Engineered Integrations Compare to Official APIs Dimension Official Public API Reverse-Engineered Integration Availability Only if the platform publishes one Any authenticated web platform Documentation Provided by the platform Generated from endpoint analysis Access requirements Partner program or approval process User account credentials Data layer stability High (published contract) High (backend API, not UI) Latency Direct HTTP Under 3 seconds (no browser) Maintenance responsibility Platform team Integration provider (Integuru) Last verified July 2026. The practical difference comes down to access and ownership. An official API exists only if the platform built and published one, which many platforms in healthcare, logistics, and property management have not done, or have done only partially. A reverse-engineered integration exists for any platform that has an authenticated web interface, which is most of them. When Reverse-Engineered Integration Is the Right Tool Four situations where it is the obvious choice: The platform has no public API. The web interface exists; the programmatic access does not. This is the most common scenario in healthcare (EHR and practice management systems), logistics (carrier portals and transport management systems), property management (lease and maintenance platforms), and legal (court filing and matter management systems). The official API is incomplete. The platform publishes a developer API, but it covers read-only access to a subset of the data your integration actually needs. The full workflow, including write operations, lives in the web interface only. A partner program takes too long. Formal API partnership programs require months of application review and enterprise contract minimums, a timeline that rarely fits the window between signing a customer and shipping the integration. You are integrating with a legacy system or government portal. Systems that predate modern API design, or that were never built for programmatic access, are unlikely to publish a developer API. Their web interface is the only programmatic surface available. If any of these describe your situation, reverse-engineered integration is not a workaround. It is the correct technical approach. title: Contractor answering service: Stop losing jobs to a missed call
summary: See why contractors lose jobs to missed calls and compare live, AI, and hybrid answering service options built for busy crews.
body_text: Answer the phone fast, and the next call becomes a booked job instead of a lost one. You’re forty feet up a ladder when the phone rings. Or elbow-deep in a clogged sink. Or driving between two job sites with 15 minutes to spare and no hands free. The call goes to voicemail, and the homeowner on the other end doesn’t wait around. They hang up and dial the next contractor in their search results, and that job is gone before you even knew it existed. This is the daily math of running a trades business: every hour on a job site is an hour the phone might ring unanswered. Office-based businesses can staff a front desk. Contractors can’t, because the work happens in trucks, crawlspaces, and other people’s homes. A receptionist can’t ride along in a truck, but every one of those calls, whether it’s a new job, angry homeowner, or a quick question, still needs someone to answer it. A contractor answering service catches that call while you’re on the ladder, so the homeowner gets a live response instead of dialing the next name on the list. Three models deliver that coverage: live answering services, AI answering services, and hybrid setups that combine both. Here’s how they compare. Key takeaway Crews on job sites can’t answer calls the way an office can AI answering services capture job details without adding office staff Emergency versus routine call triage matters as much as answer speed RingCentral AI Receptionist routes and captures every call consistently, shift to shift Why a missed call costs contractors more than a bad review A bad review stings, but it’s recoverable. A missed call usually isn’t. The homeowner with a burst pipe or a dead AC unit in July isn’t leaving a strained voicemail and waiting for a callback. They’re calling the next name that shows up, and in most markets, that takes seconds, not hours. The data backs up what every contractor already feels in their gut. Research from call analytics firm Invoca found that fewer than 3% of callers who are sent to a service business’s voicemail actually leave a message. No message means no callback, no lead, and no way to even know you lost the job. Speed matters just as much if the caller doesn’t leave a message. The caller has already searched, compared a few options, and decided that whoever answers first gets serious consideration. Responding quickly means the difference between a customer and a lost opportunity. For contractors, this urgency compounds. Service and repair calls are frequently time-sensitive by nature, so the tolerance for “we’ll call you back” is lower than in most other industries. What an answering service needs to handle for trades A dispatcher answering calls for a law firm or a dental office works a predictable rhythm: business hours, a desk, a calendar. Contractors rarely operate under those conditions. Calls come in from a truck cab, between appointments, or mid-repair, and they cover a wider range of urgency and intent than most service businesses ever deal with. An answering solution built for trades has to sort three distinct call types without slowing anyone down. Emergency and same-day repair requests A no-heat call in January or a flooding basement doesn’t fit into next week’s schedule. These callers need to know, immediately, that someone heard them and that help is coming. An answering service for contractors has to recognize urgency from the first few seconds of the conversation, whether that’s a keyword like “flooding” or “no power,” and route the call to whoever can respond fastest. Treating an emergency like a routine scheduling request costs the job and damages the kind of trust that drives referrals in trades businesses. Routine scheduling and estimates Not every call is a crisis. A homeowner wants a quote for a kitchen remodel, or a customer needs to confirm next Tuesday’s appointment. These calls need to accurately capture: Scope of work Timeline Contact details Ideally, all information is logged correctly so a callback doesn’t require the customer to repeat themselves. Basic answering services break down most often here. A rushed intake that gets the address wrong or skips the callback number turns a routine estimate request into a lost booking. Vendor and supplier calls Not every call is even from a customer. Suppliers confirming a delivery window, subcontractors checking in on a schedule change, or a permit office following up all compete for the same phone line as customer calls. An answering setup that can’t tell a supplier call from a customer lead either interrupts the crew unnecessarily or buries a real customer call under low-priority traffic. Sorting these calls correctly keeps the crew focused on the work that actually needs their attention. Live agents vs. AI answering services vs. hybrid models Contractors evaluating answering options are really choosing between three categories, and each comes with real benefits and tradeoffs. Live answering services These services route calls to trained human agents, typically working from scripts for common scenarios. Benefits Live agents handle nuance and can improvise on unusual requests in ways a script can’t anticipate. This includes talking a panicked homeowner through a gas leak, negotiating a same-day slot for a VIP client, or catching that a “routine” call is actually an emergency based on tone alone. Trained agents working from scripts cover common scenarios well, and a good agent who knows your business can quote accurately, cross-sell a maintenance plan, or recognize a repeat customer without pulling up a file. Tradeoffs Live agents cost more per call than automated options. That cost sometimes buys inconsistent quality since it varies by agent and by how well that agent actually knows your business, your service area, and your pricing. Turnover at the answering service means you’re periodically paying to get new agents up to speed. Storm season or a summer heat wave can overwhelm live services the same way it overwhelms an in-house team: call volume spikes, agents get pulled thin, and callers end up back in a queue exactly when they need a fast answer most. AI answering services AI answering services answer every call the same way, at any hour, without hold times or agent turnover. Benefits Cost per call is generally lower and predictable, since there’s no staffing to scale up during busy stretches, no overtime for after-hours calls, and no ramp-up time for a new hire learning your services and pricing. This category has matured enough that context-aware systems no longer feel like the rigid phone trees your customers have learned to distrust. They can pull from a knowledge base to answer service-area or pricing questions, schedule appointments directly into a calendar, and flag urgent jobs (a burst pipe, no heat in freezing weather) for immediate callback instead of routing them into a generic queue. Tradeoffs AI handles structured scenarios (booking, triage, lead capture) well, but unusual or highly emotional calls may still need a human handoff. A caller describing a multi-part problem, negotiating a quote, or venting about a botched job can push the system past what it can handle without a human handoff. Contractors relying on AI alone need a clear fallback (a live transfer option or a same-day callback promise) so those calls don’t dead-end. Hybrid models Hybrid models pair AI for first contact and routine capture with live agents for complex or high-stakes calls. This combines the consistency of AI with a human safety net. Benefits AI answers immediately and captures the basics: caller name, job type, address, and urgency, so nothing gets missed during off-hours or call spikes. Live agents step in for the calls that actually need judgment: an angry customer, a pricing negotiation, or a job that doesn’t fit the standard categories. Contractors get consistent intake around the clock without losing the human touch on calls where it matters most. Tradeoffs This can be the most expensive option, since it layers live agent costs on top of an AI system. It also requires clear escalation rules. Contractors have to define upfront which call types trigger a handoff to a live agent, and vague rules lead to either too many unnecessary handoffs (driving up cost) or too few (leaving complex calls stuck with the bot). Setup takes more coordination than either standalone option. For a contractor deciding between these, the right fit depends on call volume, crew size, and how often calls fall outside routine scheduling and emergency triage. What separates basic call answering from real job capture Answering the phone is the easy part. Turning that call into a job on the schedule is where most answering services, live or automated, fall short. The gap shows up in three places: Accuracy of the details captured How fast the lead gets followed up on Whether the process holds up across multiple crews or trucks Transcribing an address wrong, dropping a callback number, or writing a job description too vague to act on can turn even an answered call into a wasted one. This kind of mishandling doesn’t show up in call-answer-rate metrics, but contractors who track it closely tend to find it’s just as costly as calls that go unanswered outright. Follow-up speed matters as much as capture accuracy. Logging a job detail correctly but sitting on it for six hours is nearly as costly as a call that went to voicemail, given how quickly homeowners move on to the next option. Consistency across trucks and crews is where a lot of basic answering setups break down. A system that works well for one crew’s schedule but creates confusion for a second or third truck isn’t actually solving the problem. It’s just moving it. This is the real benchmark for evaluating how your trades business can effectively use any answering service: not whether it answers, but whether it reliably turns a call into accurate, actionable, timely job information regardless of which crew, which shift, or which truck is handling service at the moment. How RingCentral AI Receptionist handles contractor call volume Contractors don’t have a front desk. Crews are in the field, trucks are on the road, and calls come in whether or not anyone is available to answer them. That’s when RingCentral AI Receptionist (AIR) becomes your ideal solution. AIR answers every incoming call automatically, so a call during a busy install or a late-night emergency doesn’t just ring out to voicemail. Instead of forcing callers through a rigid menu of numbered options, AIR uses context-aware routing to understand what the caller needs and directs the call accordingly, whether that’s an emergency repair request or a routine scheduling question. For the calls that turn into business, AIR captures lead details automatically, so job information doesn’t depend on whoever happens to answer the phone or how clearly they hear it over shop noise. AIR also supports appointment scheduling directly through the call, giving customers a booked time without a callback loop. Because AIR handles every call the same way, it captures and routes intake consistently across every shift, every location, and every crew, solving the exact inconsistency problem that makes basic answering setups unreliable at scale. Get every call answered, not just some of them Consistent call handling is now a baseline expectation, the same way customers expect a quote within a day or a truck to show up on time. Which model fits best—live, AI, or hybrid—comes down to your crew size, your call volume, and how much of your business runs on emergency versus routine work. The contractors winning more jobs aren’t the ones with the biggest crews. They’re the ones whose phone never goes unanswered. See how RingCentral AI Receptionist handles that for trades businesses of any size. FAQs about contractor answering services Do contractors need a 24/7 answering service? Most contractors benefit from around-the-clock coverage, especially in trades with emergency call volume like plumbing, HVAC, and electrical work. A burst pipe or a no-heat call doesn’t wait for business hours, and the contractor who answers at 11 p.m. often gets the job by default. What is the difference between a live and an AI contractor answering service? A live answering service routes calls to trained human agents, which handles unusual requests well, but costs more and can struggle to keep up during volume spikes. An AI answering service answers every call the same way at any hour, at a lower and more predictable cost per call, with less flexibility for highly unusual scenarios. Can an AI answering service schedule jobs for contractors? Yes. Modern AI answering services, including RingCentral AI Receptionist , support appointment scheduling directly during the call, so a customer can get a booked time without a separate callback. How much does a contractor answering service typically cost? Cost varies by call volume and model. Live answering services generally charge more per call or per minute due to staffing costs, while AI answering services typically offer flat or usage-based pricing that stays predictable even as call volume grows during busy seasons. Originally published Jul 22, 2026
